title: Talk to Her
full_review:
Two women in comas and the men who love them are the subject of Spanish writer-director Pedro Almodovar's moving but problematic "Talk to Her" (Sony Classics).

Jumping back and forth in time, we learn that Benigno (Javier Camara), a sweet-natured male nurse, could see dancer Alicia (Leonor Watling) taking ballet lessons from his apartment window, and, smitten with her, unsuccessfully tried to befriend her.

However, a car accident put her in a deep coma and for four years he has devotedly cared for her, speaking with her and hoping she will respond.

One day he sees Marco (Dario Grandinetti) visiting his comatose girlfriend at the hospital and remembers sitting beside him at a dance performance and being touched by how tears trailed down the man's face. Benigno introduces himself and a supportive friendship based on their shared situation develops.

Marco's girlfriend is bullfighter Lydia (Rosario Flores), who had just been dumped by her famed bullfighter lover (Adolfo Fernandez) when writer Marco interviewed her -- and the two became romantically involved. Her coma resulted from being gored, and Marco feels guilty that she may have been distracted by problems in their relationship.

The filmmaker captures the beautiful melancholy tone of the film with its tragedy and tenderness, longing and loneliness. And he masterfully interweaves other art forms such as the dance and haunting music to underline the delicacy of feelings being explored. Almodovar is always a bit sexually outrageous, and here he incorporates a short silent film meant as metaphor in which a man is miniaturized, runs across his naked wife's body and seeks the safety of her womb by diving between her legs -- a surreal scene not for everyone's taste.

Yet what is most disturbing involves now giving away the plot to explain why a sensitive film falls into morally offensive territory.

In hopes the shock of labor will awaken Alicia, Benigno rapes and impregnates his helpless patient. Although the baby is stillborn, Alicia does return to consciousness. For the crime Benigno is sent to prison, where he chooses to commit suicide. One feels great sympathy for the wrongheaded nurse, but his actions are seen less as rape than as a grand romantic gesture and his suicide as selflessly sacrificial. And so, despite the touching performances and the lyrical presentation of the story, romanticizing rape and suicide goes beyond what the Catholic audience can embrace.

Subtitles.

Due to some bizarre sexual situations with nudity, brief violence, an off-screen rape, suicide and a few instances of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
